title: Genesis 13 — The return from Mitsrayim and the separation from Lot

verdicts.reasoning: Direct rendering of va-yaal Avram mi-Mitsrayim. The chain of subjects (he, his wife, all that he had, Lot) tracks the Hebrew word-for-word; ha-Negbah as 'toward the Negev' is the standard directional-he. No divergence from consensus.

citations: BDB s.v. kbd 'be heavy, weighty; rich'
verdicts.reasoning: Kaved m'od literally 'very heavy' with the b- prepositional phrases naming the wealth-substances. The literal 'heavy in cattle, in silver, and in gold' preserves the Hebrew idiom rather than smoothing to 'rich'; defensible and matches ASV.

Editor follows the qere (oholo, 'his tent'), which is the masoretic-consensus reading and matches the consistent Genesis idiom (12:8, 18:1, 26:25, 31:25). Commentary records the three circulating readings of the ketiv and the standard rationale for following the qere. Correct.

Standard rendering of mqom ha-mizbeach asher asah sham ba-rishonah and the qara b-shem YHWH formula. The formula is already tracked by the existing glossary entry; commentary correctly locates the Bethel-altar return as the structural close of the descent-and-return frame opened at 12:8.
Routine narrative bridge; the participial ha-holekh et-Avram ('who went with Abram') is rendered straightforwardly. tson u-vaqar v-ohalim ('flocks and herds and tents') is literal.

citations: BDB s.v. nasa II 'bear up, endure, support'
verdicts.reasoning: v-lo nasa otam ha-aretz uses nasa in the 'support / bear up' sense — the standard idiom for land-carrying-capacity. 'And the land was not able to bear them' is the consensus rendering (ASV, NRSV, NJPS); the verse's internal repetition (lashevet yachdav twice) is preserved.

citations: Cassuto, Commentary on Genesis II, 1944/1961, p. 326
verdicts.reasoning: The participial-progressive 'were then dwelling in the land' preserves the temporal force of yoshev + az without committing to a definitive source-critical position. Note the singular participle yoshev governs the conjoined ethnic terms collectively — standard Hebrew syntax. The Documentary Hypothesis reading is correctly held as well-attested but not universal in the glossary rationale.

citations: Alter, Five Books of Moses, 2004, p. 65 (on anashim achim anachnu)
verdicts.reasoning: 'Men who are brothers' is the literal anashim achim anachnu and matches ASV. 'Kinsmen' would be the smoother idiomatic alternative (so NRSV, NJPS) but the literal preserves the doubled anashim + achim that Alter flags. Defensible.

The chiastic left-right / right-left phrasing of im-ha-s'mol v-eminah v-im-ha-yamin v-asm'ilah is preserved in the English. Hipared na me-alai as 'separate yourself, please, from me' uses the standard niphal of p-r-d (be separated). Routine.

citations: Alter, Five Books of Moses, 2004, p. 65
verdicts.reasoning: The doubled simile k-gan YHWH k-eretz Mitsrayim is preserved literally. The Eden back-reference is grammatically explicit (gan + YHWH binds 13:10 to 2:8) and the Eden/Sodom typology is mainstream-critical territory cited by all five named commentators. The single WoH-posture sentence sits in the glossary rationale (not in the translated text); the translated English is defensible to any scholar reading it cold.

va-yissa Lot mi-qedem rendered 'journeyed eastward' (matching ASV, NRSV). mi-qedem literally 'from the east' but contextually directional; Sarna notes the eastward = away-from-Eden resonance with Gen 3:24 va-yashken mi-qedem l-gan-Eden. va-yipardu ish me-al achiv preserves the separation-formula.

Standard rendering. va-ye'ehal ad-Sdom ('pitched his tent as far as Sodom') uses the rare denominative verb of ohel ('tent'); 'pitched his tent as far as Sodom' is the consensus rendering (ASV, NRSV, NJPS). The narrative-foreshadowing function of the closing toward Sodom is implicit and properly left to commentary on the Sodom destruction-cycle.

The dative-l with chata'im is grammatically standard for 'sinners against [someone]' (cf. Gen 39:9 v-chatati l-Elohim; Exod 10:16; Num 32:23 chata'tem la-YHWH). 'Sinners against YHWH exceedingly' matches ASV; Speiser and HALOT both treat the l- construction as the normal idiom. The doubled epithet ra'im v-chata'im and the m'od intensifier are correctly handled in commentary. Editor's decision to forgo a separate glossary entry is sound.

va-YHWH amar (not va-yera) correctly noted in commentary — auditory rather than visual mode of revelation. The sa-na eynekha u-re'eh formula is rendered 'lift up now your eyes and look' (matches ASV). The four-direction tsafonah va-negbah va-qedmah va-yammah is preserved. The patriarchal-formula scope (12 verses) in the new glossary entry is appropriate.

Reissue and expansion of the 12:7 seed-land promise into a to-you + to-your-seed binary with ad-olam ('forever'). The translation preserves the doubled l-kha + u-l-zar'akha distribution. Already tracked by existing zera-eretz-promise glossary entry; correctly cross-referenced.

citations: Alter, Five Books of Moses, 2004, p. 66
verdicts.reasoning: 'As the dust of the earth' is literal ka-afar ha-aretz and matches ASV. The 'if a man can count... then your seed shall be counted' conditional preserves the Hebrew yimaneh passive niphal. Hamilton's Gen 2:7 / 3:19 creation-recall reading is preserved in commentary and rationale. The consolidated triad glossary entry is sound editorial judgment.

qum hit'hallekh ba-aretz l-orkah u-l-rochbah rendered 'Arise, walk through the land in the length of it and in the breadth of it' (matches ASV). The hithpael iterative-reflexive force is preserved. The covenant-walking-as-juridical-act framing is held as inferred — the modern scholarly synthesis going back to Daube 1947 §3, followed by Speiser, Sarna, Westermann, Wenham. Holding appliesTo[] to currently-translated corpus (not adding Josh 1:3, 18:8, Deut 11:24 retroactively) is the right policy.

'Oaks of Mamre' (plural construct elonei + proper name Mamre) is rendered following ASV; LXX δρῦς supports the oak rendering. The site is correctly held as distinct from elon-Moreh (12:6) — different proper name, different geographical location, different recurrence-set. Botanical precision (oak vs. terebinth, with NJPS 'terebinths') is not load-bearing for the verse. The forward-loaded appliesTo[] scope across 10 Abraham-cycle verses is appropriate policy for a recurring proper-name site.

citations: Cassuto, Commentary on Genesis II, 1944/1961, p. 326
Kitchen, On the Reliability of the Old Testament, 2003
glossaryReview.reasoning: claim_type=inferred is correct: the Documentary Hypothesis reading is mainstream-but-not-universal critical-scholarly synthesis, not lexical fact. The rationale fairly presents both J-stratum (Wellhausen, Gunkel, von Rad, Speiser) and pre-conquest (Cassuto, Kitchen) readings without taking a definitive position. Retroactive scope to 12:6 is appropriate — the lemma is identical in form (singular Canaanite there, doubled here) and the parenthetical does the same work in both.

citations: Alter, Five Books of Moses, 2004, p. 65
glossaryReview.reasoning: claim_type=direct is correct: the lexical back-reference (gan + YHWH at 13:10 binding to gan b-Eden at 2:8) is grammatically explicit and the inter-textual reading is the scholarly consensus across all five named commentators. The WoH posture is held to a single sentence in the rationale ('Gen 1 and Gen 2-3 are taken as describing a single project-beginning context') — visible-in-rationale but not-arguing-the-cosmology, which is the right register. No lens leakage in the translated text itself.

claim_type=direct is correct: the nasa eynayim formula occurrences are uncontested lexical fact at each of the 12 cited patriarchal-Genesis verses. The recurrence-set is comprehensive for the Abraham-Isaac-Jacob-Joseph arc; holding the scope to patriarchal Genesis for v2.10.0 (rather than expanding to Psalms, Prophets) is appropriate corpus-staging policy.

citations: Alter, Five Books of Moses, 2004, p. 66
glossaryReview.reasoning: claim_type=direct is correct: the three comparisons (dust 13:16, stars 15:5, sand 22:17) are grammatically explicit at their cited verses. Consolidating into one entry rather than three is sound editorial judgment — preserves the cosmographic earth/sky/shore distribution as a single insight rather than fragmenting it. Hamilton's Gen 2:7 / 3:19 creation-recall reading of the dust-image preserved. appliesTo[] scope (5 verses: 13:16, 15:5, 22:17, 26:4, 32:13) correctly distinguishes the triad itself from later cross-corpus citations of it.

claim_type=inferred is correct: the covenantal-walking-as-juridical-act framing (Roman usucapio / Anglo-Saxon seisin / German Begehungsritus) is modern scholarly synthesis going back to Daube 1947 §3, not lexical fact. The rationale correctly distinguishes this juridical-spatial sense of the hithpael (13:17, Josh 18:8) from the ethical-relational walking-before-Elohim sense (Gen 3:8, 5:22, 6:9, 17:1, etc.). Holding appliesTo[] to the single currently-translated verse and noting Josh 1:3 / 18:8 / Deut 11:24 in the rationale only is the right corpus-staging policy.

claim_type=direct is correct: the proper-name phrase elonei Mamre is grammatically explicit at every cited verse and the site-identification is uncontested. Correctly held as parallel-to-but-distinct-from elon-Moreh (12:6) — different proper name, different geographical location, different recurrence-set; the Translator's framing-brief correction was rightly sustained. Both classical historical reading (Sarna, Wenham — Mamre as Amorite contemporary) and aetiological reading (Westermann — pre-existing place-name) cited. Forward-loaded appliesTo[] scope across 10 Abraham-cycle verses is appropriate for a recurring proper-name site. Botanical question (oak vs. terebinth) handled fairly with ASV 'oaks' chosen for consistency with 12:6.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּעַל֩ אַבְרָ֨ם מִמִּצְרַ֜יִם ה֠וּא וְאִשְׁתּ֧וֹ וְכָל־אֲשֶׁר־ל֛וֹ וְל֥וֹט עִמּ֖וֹ הַנֶּֽגְבָּה׃

i18n.en: Abram went up from Mitsrayim, he and his wife and all that he had, and Lot with him, toward the Negev.

paragraphs.text: וְאַבְרָ֖ם כָּבֵ֣ד מְאֹ֑ד בַּמִּקְנֶ֕ה בַּכֶּ֖סֶף וּבַזָּהָֽב׃

i18n.en: And Abram was very heavy in cattle, in silver, and in gold.

paragraphs.text: וַיֵּ֙לֶךְ֙ לְמַסָּעָ֔יו מִנֶּ֖גֶב וְעַד־בֵּֽית־אֵ֑ל עַד־הַמָּק֗וֹם אֲשֶׁר־הָ֨יָה שָׁ֤ם אהלה [אָֽהֳלוֹ֙] בַּתְּחִלָּ֔ה בֵּ֥ין בֵּֽית־אֵ֖ל וּבֵ֥ין הָעָֽי׃

i18n.en: He went on his journeys from the Negev as far as Bethel, to the place where his tent had been at the beginning, between Bethel and Ai,

paragraphs.commentary: **A ketiv/qere divergence sits at the center of the verse.** The consonantal text (*ketiv*) reads אהלה — without a final *mater lectionis* — which the Masoretes pointed in the margin (*qere*) as אָהֳלוֹ, *oholo*, 'his tent' (masculine-singular noun + 3ms pronominal suffix). The qere is the standard masculine-singular construct-with-suffix form and matches the consistent Genesis idiom (cf. Gen 12:8, 18:1, 18:10, 26:25, 31:25). Two minority readings of the unpointed *ketiv* circulate: as a defectively-written *oholah* (feminine, 'her tent' — Sarai's tent), or as an archaic spelling of the same masculine form preserved without the conventional waw. The Masoretes' qere is the consensus reading and the WoH translation follows it ('his tent'), matching ASV, NJPS, and NRSV.

paragraphs.text: אֶל־מְקוֹם֙ הַמִּזְבֵּ֔חַ אֲשֶׁר־עָ֥שָׂה שָׁ֖ם בָּרִאשֹׁנָ֑ה וַיִּקְרָ֥א שָׁ֛ם אַבְרָ֖ם בְּשֵׁ֥ם יְהוָֽה׃

i18n.en: to the place of the altar that he had made there at the first; and Abram called there on the name of YHWH.

paragraphs.commentary: **The Bethel-altar return is the structural close of the Mitsrayim descent-and-return frame.** The chapter is deliberately bracketing the famine-and-descent episode of 12:10–20 between two altar-callings at Bethel — the inaugural altar of 12:8 (*qara b-shem YHWH* there for the first time on the land) and this restored altar at the same site. The phrase *barishonah* (at the first / formerly) is the chapter's own backward gesture: Abram is returning not just to a region but to a specific cult-place and resuming an interrupted relationship. The *qara b-shem YHWH* formula carries the antediluvian Seth-Enosh cult-resumption claim across the patriarchal narratives; the glossary entry tracks the formula's recurrences.

paragraphs.text: וְגַם־לְל֔וֹט הַהֹלֵ֖ךְ אֶת־אַבְרָ֑ם הָיָ֥ה צֹאן־וּבָקָ֖ר וְאֹהָלִֽים׃

i18n.en: And Lot also, who went with Abram, had flocks and herds and tents.

paragraphs.text: וְלֹא־נָשָׂ֥א אֹתָ֛ם הָאָ֖רֶץ לָשֶׁ֣בֶת יַחְדָּ֑ו כִּֽי־הָיָ֤ה רְכוּשָׁם֙ רָ֔ב וְלֹ֥א יָֽכְל֖וּ לָשֶׁ֥בֶת יַחְדָּֽו׃

i18n.en: And the land was not able to bear them, that they might dwell together; for their substance was great, and they could not dwell together.

paragraphs.text: וַֽיְהִי־רִ֗יב בֵּ֚ין רֹעֵ֣י מִקְנֵֽה־אַבְרָ֔ם וּבֵ֖ין רֹעֵ֣י מִקְנֵה־ל֑וֹט וְהַֽכְּנַעֲנִי֙ וְהַפְּרִזִּ֔י אָ֖ז יֹשֵׁ֥ב בָּאָֽרֶץ׃

i18n.en: And there was strife between the herders of Abram's cattle and the herders of Lot's cattle. And the Canaanite and the Perizzite were then dwelling in the land.

paragraphs.commentary: **The verse closes with the chapter's most-cited Documentary-Hypothesis flag.** *V-ha-Kna'ani v-ha-Prizi az yoshev ba-aretz* — 'and the Canaanite and the Perizzite were then dwelling in the land' — is a temporal-perspective parenthetical that foregrounds a redactional vantage *later than* the events described. The participial *yoshev* (dwelling) with the temporal adverb *az* (then) reads as a narrator's aside to a reader for whom the Canaanites and Perizzites are no longer the dominant population: the parenthetical only does work if it informs the audience of a state of affairs they would not have assumed by default. // **The verse pairs with the simpler parallel at Gen 12:6** — *v-ha-Kna'ani az ba-aretz* — which uses the Canaanite alone. The expanded inventory here at 13:7 doubles it with the Perizzite, anticipating the longer ethnographic lists that will appear at 15:18–21 and 34:30 and across Deuteronomy and Joshua. The doubling has been read as either a redactional expansion of the 12:6 form (so Westermann, *Genesis 12–36*, Hermeneia 1985) or as a context-specific shift naming the two peoples Abram and Lot's herders would have been in direct competition with for grazing-rights in the hill country (so Wenham, *WBC Genesis 1–15*, 1987, p. 297). // **The Documentary Hypothesis reading** treats both notices (12:6 and 13:7) as J-stratum parentheticals from a post-conquest perspective. The reading is mainstream in critical scholarship (Wellhausen, Gunkel, von Rad, Speiser) but not universally accepted; Cassuto and Kitchen have argued that the parentheticals are compatible with a pre-conquest narrator describing the ethnographic situation of the patriarchs' own day, where the Canaanite-Perizzite presence was the salient feature of land-use competition. The WoH translation preserves the parenthetical's temporal force ('were then dwelling') without taking a definitive source-critical position; the redactional-seam reading is well-attested but the dating question remains open.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר אַבְרָ֜ם אֶל־ל֗וֹט אַל־נָ֨א תְהִ֤י מְרִיבָה֙ בֵּינִ֣י וּבֵינֶ֔יךָ וּבֵ֥ין רֹעַ֖י וּבֵ֣ין רֹעֶ֑יךָ כִּֽי־אֲנָשִׁ֥ים אַחִ֖ים אֲנָֽחְנוּ׃

i18n.en: Abram said to Lot, "Let there be no strife, please, between me and you, and between my herders and your herders; for we are men who are brothers.

paragraphs.text: הֲלֹ֤א כָל־הָאָ֙רֶץ֙ לְפָנֶ֔יךָ הִפָּ֥רֶד נָ֖א מֵעָלָ֑י אִם־הַשְּׂמֹ֣אל וְאֵימִ֔נָה וְאִם־הַיָּמִ֖ין וְאַשְׂמְאִֽילָה׃

i18n.en: Is not the whole land before you? Separate yourself, please, from me. If you go to the left, then I will go to the right; and if you go to the right, then I will go to the left."

paragraphs.text: וַיִּשָּׂא־ל֣וֹט אֶת־עֵינָ֗יו וַיַּרְא֙ אֶת־כָּל־כִּכַּ֣ר הַיַּרְדֵּ֔ן כִּ֥י כֻלָּ֖הּ מַשְׁקֶ֑ה לִפְנֵ֣י ׀ שַׁחֵ֣ת יְהוָ֗ה אֶת־סְדֹם֙ וְאֶת־עֲמֹרָ֔ה כְּגַן־יְהוָה֙ כְּאֶ֣רֶץ מִצְרַ֔יִם בֹּאֲכָ֖ה צֹֽעַר׃

i18n.en: Lot lifted up his eyes and saw all the plain of the Jordan, that it was well watered everywhere — before YHWH destroyed Sodom and Amorah — like the garden of YHWH, like the land of Mitsrayim, as you go toward Tsoar.

paragraphs.commentary: **The verse contains the chapter's most consequential inter-textual move.** *K-gan YHWH k-eretz Mitsrayim* — 'like the garden of YHWH, like the land of Mitsrayim' — is a doubled simile that yokes two of the Hebrew Bible's most freighted geographical referents to the pre-destruction plain of the Jordan. // **First, *gan YHWH*.** The phrase is a lexical back-reference to *gan b-Eden* of Gen 2:8 — the only other 'garden' associated with YHWH-Elohim in the primeval narratives. The reading is mainstream: Westermann (*Genesis 12–36*, 1985, p. 178), Sarna (*JPS Genesis*, 1989, p. 100), Hamilton (*NICOT Genesis 1–17*, 1990, p. 393), and Alter (*Five Books of Moses*, 2004, p. 65) all flag the Eden allusion. The phrase frames the Jordan plain as a second Eden — a primeval-fertility analogue — and sets up the narrative engine that the next several chapters will run on: Lot has chosen the Eden-like region precisely when YHWH is about to destroy it. The narrator's parenthetical *lifnei shachet YHWH et-Sodom v-et-Amorah* ('before YHWH destroyed Sodom and Amorah') makes the typology explicit by name. // **The Eden-loss / Sodom-destruction parallel** that Genesis stages across chs 2–3 and chs 18–19 is one of the corpus's clearest type-scene pairings: a fertile divinely-favored region, a human action that violates its terms, expulsion-and-destruction, and a flaming sword (Gen 3:24) / fire-and-sulfur from the skies (Gen 19:24). The reading is critical-consensus and pre-dates the modern literary-critical turn (von Rad, *Genesis*, 1972 ET, p. 173). // **Second, *eretz Mitsrayim*.** The Nile-delta comparison stages a different resonance: the Jordan plain is a Nile-grade agricultural prototype, irrigated and produce-rich, the model the wilderness generation will remember nostalgically (Num 11:5, *we remember the fish we ate in Mitsrayim freely, the cucumbers and the melons and the leeks and the onions and the garlic*). Lot is choosing on Mitsrayim-grade criteria — the same evaluative frame that drew Abram down to Egypt in the famine of 12:10 — and the chapter is structurally rhyming his choice with Abram's earlier descent. // The WoH translation preserves the doubled simile literally ('like the garden of YHWH, like the land of Mitsrayim'), matching ASV. The Eden back-reference and the Sodom destruction-cycle typology are tracked by the *gan-yhwh-eden-back-reference* glossary entry.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּבְחַר־ל֣וֹ ל֗וֹט אֵ֚ת כָּל־כִּכַּ֣ר הַיַּרְדֵּ֔ן וַיִּסַּ֥ע ל֖וֹט מִקֶּ֑דֶם וַיִּפָּ֣רְד֔וּ אִ֖ישׁ מֵעַ֥ל אָחִֽיו׃

i18n.en: Lot chose for himself all the plain of the Jordan, and Lot journeyed eastward; and they separated themselves the one from the other.

paragraphs.text: אַבְרָ֖ם יָשַׁ֣ב בְּאֶֽרֶץ־כְּנָ֑עַן וְל֗וֹט יָשַׁב֙ בְּעָרֵ֣י הַכִּכָּ֔ר וַיֶּאֱהַ֖ל עַד־סְדֹֽם׃

i18n.en: Abram dwelt in the land of Canaan, and Lot dwelt in the cities of the plain and pitched his tent as far as Sodom.

paragraphs.text: וְאַנְשֵׁ֣י סְדֹ֔ם רָעִ֖ים וְחַטָּאִ֑ים לַיהוָ֖ה מְאֹֽד׃

i18n.en: And the men of Sodom were wicked and sinners against YHWH exceedingly.

paragraphs.commentary: **The verse is a narrator-editorial intrusion that foreshadows chs 18–19.** Two features make the assertion rhetorically pointed. // **First, the doubled epithet** *ra'im v-chata'im* — 'wicked and sinners'. *Ra'im* (from r-a-a, 'be bad / evil') names the moral-quality term: the men *were* bad. *Chata'im* (from ch-t-a, 'to miss the mark, to fail in obligation, to sin') names the relational-juridical term: they had failed against someone. The pairing collapses character and action — they were both the kind of people and the doers of the kind of acts. // **Second, the dative *l-YHWH*.** Hebrew has two standard ways to mark the offended party of a sin: *neged* (against, adversative — cf. 1 Sam 12:23, 'far be it from me that I should sin against [*neged*] YHWH') and *l-* + name (dative — cf. Gen 39:9, *v-chatati l-Elohim*, 'and I would have sinned against Elohim'; Exod 10:16, 'I have sinned against [*l-*] YHWH your Elohim'; Num 32:23, *u-vatem chata'tem la-YHWH*, 'and you have sinned against YHWH'). The *l-* + divine name with *chata'im* is grammatically standard for 'sinners against [someone]', so the construction itself is unremarkable. Speiser (*Anchor Bible Genesis*, 1964, p. 99) and HALOT both treat it as the normal Hebrew idiom. // **What is more loaded is the *me'od* intensifier at the verse's end.** The flat-assertion register — 'were wicked and sinners against YHWH *exceedingly*' — pairs the verse with the corpus's other narrator-editorial intrusions of moral judgment: Gen 6:5 (*v-yar YHWH ki rabbah ra'at ha-adam ba-aretz v-khol-yetzer machshvot libo raq ra kol-ha-yom*, 'YHWH saw that the wickedness of humanity was great in the earth, and every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually') and Gen 6:11–12 (*v-tishachet ha-aretz lifnei ha-Elohim*, 'and the earth was corrupt before the Elohim'). The verse is doing scene-setting work for the destruction of chs 18–19, framing it as a judgment on a community whose wickedness has been editorially established in advance. The WoH translation reads 'sinners against YHWH exceedingly', matching ASV; the dative-l construction is preserved without flagging a separate glossary entry.

paragraphs.text: וַֽיהוָ֞ה אָמַ֣ר אֶל־אַבְרָ֗ם אַחֲרֵי֙ הִפָּֽרֶד־ל֣וֹט מֵֽעִמּ֔וֹ שָׂ֣א נָ֤א עֵינֶ֙יךָ֙ וּרְאֵ֔ה מִן־הַמָּק֖וֹם אֲשֶׁר־אַתָּ֣ה שָׁ֑ם צָפֹ֥נָה וָנֶ֖גְבָּה וָקֵ֥דְמָה וָיָֽמָּה׃

i18n.en: And YHWH said to Abram, after Lot had separated himself from him, "Lift up now your eyes and look from the place where you are, northward and southward and eastward and westward;

paragraphs.commentary: **The verse uses the *va-YHWH amar* formula** — *and YHWH said* — rather than the patriarchal-theophany formula *va-yera YHWH* of 12:7 and 17:1. The distinction is meaningful: at 12:7 and 18:1 YHWH *was seen / appeared* (niphal of r-a-h); here YHWH simply *speaks* without the mode of seeing being specified. The chapter is staging the address as an auditory revelation rather than a visual theophany — the *sa eynekha* imperative that follows asks Abram to lift his own eyes, not to look upon a visible YHWH. // **The phrase *sa-na eynekha u-re'eh*** — 'lift up, please, your eyes and look' — is the inaugural occurrence of the *nasa eynayim* (lift one's eyes) formula in the patriarchal corpus. The formula recurs at Gen 18:2 (Abraham sees the three visitors at Mamre), Gen 22:4 (Abraham sees the place of the binding from afar), Gen 22:13 (Abraham sees the ram), Gen 24:63 (Isaac at evening), Gen 31:10 and 31:12 (Jacob's dream-vision), Gen 33:1 and 33:5 (Jacob sees Esau and the family), Gen 37:25 (Joseph's brothers see the caravan), Gen 43:29 (Joseph sees Benjamin). The formula is the standard Genesis seeing-formula, often introducing a visionary or recognitional perception. Westermann (*Genesis 12–36*, 1985, p. 180) notes the formulaic character; Alter (2004) flags the consistent use across the patriarchal arc. The WoH translation preserves the verb-phrase 'lift up your eyes' across all occurrences; the glossary entry tracks the full recurrence-set.

paragraphs.text: כִּ֧י אֶת־כָּל־הָאָ֛רֶץ אֲשֶׁר־אַתָּ֥ה רֹאֶ֖ה לְךָ֣ אֶתְּנֶ֑נָּה וּֽלְזַרְעֲךָ֖ עַד־עוֹלָֽם׃

i18n.en: for all the land that you see, to you I will give it, and to your seed forever.

paragraphs.commentary: **The verse reissues and expands the seed-land promise of 12:7.** The 12:7 formula (*l-zarakha eten et-ha-aretz ha-zot*) is here doubled into a *to you* + *to your seed* binary, and the new modifier *ad-olam* ('forever / for an indefinite duration') is added. The expansion is the second iteration in the Genesis covenantal chain that will run through 15:7-21 (cut-covenant ritual), 17:7-8 (*brit olam*), 22:17 (the doubled stars-and-sand image), 26:3-4 (to Isaac), 28:13-14 (to Jacob), and 35:11-12. The *zera-eretz-promise* glossary entry tracks the full chain.

paragraphs.text: וְשַׂמְתִּ֥י אֶֽת־זַרְעֲךָ֖ כַּעֲפַ֣ר הָאָ֑רֶץ אֲשֶׁ֣ר ׀ אִם־יוּכַ֣ל אִ֗ישׁ לִמְנוֹת֙ אֶת־עֲפַ֣ר הָאָ֔רֶץ גַּֽם־זַרְעֲךָ֖ יִמָּנֶֽה׃

i18n.en: And I will make your seed as the dust of the earth, so that if a man can count the dust of the earth, then your seed also shall be counted.

paragraphs.commentary: **The seed-like-dust comparison is the first of three patriarchal seed-comparisons.** The three are *dust of the earth* (Gen 13:16, here), *stars of the heavens* (Gen 15:5), and *sand on the seashore* (Gen 22:17, paired with the stars). The triad spans a deliberate cosmographic distribution: dust (earth, immanent, lowly), stars (sky, transcendent, height), sand (shore, the threshold between dry land and sea). Sarna (*JPS Genesis*, 1989, p. 100) and Alter (2004, p. 66) both treat the three as a deliberate set; Hamilton (*NICOT Genesis 1–17*, 1990, p. 396) reads the dust-image specifically as recalling Gen 2:7 and 3:19 — the *afar min ha-adamah* from which humanity was shaped and to which it returns. The dust-comparison here is therefore not just a multiplicity-image but a creation-recall: the patriarch's seed will share the substance of the original adamic forming-material. // The WoH translation preserves 'as the dust of the earth' (matching ASV); the *patriarchal-seed-comparison-triad* glossary entry tracks the three comparisons across the corpus.

paragraphs.text: ק֚וּם הִתְהַלֵּ֣ךְ בָּאָ֔רֶץ לְאָרְכָּ֖הּ וּלְרָחְבָּ֑הּ כִּ֥י לְךָ֖ אֶתְּנֶֽנָּה׃

i18n.en: Arise, walk through the land in the length of it and in the breadth of it; for to you I will give it."

paragraphs.commentary: **The verse names a juridical-symbolic act.** *Qum hit'hallekh ba-aretz l-orkah ul-rochbah* — 'arise, walk through the land in its length and in its breadth' — uses the hithpael of h-l-k (walk-about, traverse-iteratively) with *ba-aretz* (in the land). The construction has been read across the modern critical tradition as a covenantal taking-possession by traversal: the patriarch's walking the boundaries of the land *is itself* a legal act of taking title to it. // **The reading goes back to David Daube's *Studies in Biblical Law* (1947), §3** — comparing the rite to the Roman *usucapio* and to the Anglo-Saxon *seisin*-by-perambulation — and has been adopted by Speiser (*Anchor Bible Genesis*, 1964, p. 100), Sarna (*JPS Genesis*, 1989, p. 101), and Wenham (*WBC Genesis 1–15*, 1987, p. 299). The German biblical-law tradition discusses the same rite under the term *Begehungsritus* (boundary-walking ceremony). The parallel formulae at Josh 1:3 (*kol-makom asher tidrokh kaf-raglekhem bo lakhem n'tatiyv*, 'every place where the sole of your foot shall tread, to you have I given it') and Josh 18:8 (*qumu v-hit'halku ba-aretz v-kitvu otah*, 'arise, walk through the land and describe it') name the same juridical-symbolic act in the conquest setting. Deut 11:24 reiterates the foot-treading possession-formula. // The WoH translation preserves 'walk through the land', matching ASV; the covenant-walking reading is tracked by the *hithallech-ba-aretz-covenant-walking* glossary entry. The reading is held as *inferred* — the juridical-act framing is the modern scholarly synthesis rather than an explicit statement in the text.

paragraphs.text: וַיֶּאֱהַ֣ל אַבְרָ֗ם וַיָּבֹ֛א וַיֵּ֛שֶׁב בְּאֵלֹנֵ֥י מַמְרֵ֖א אֲשֶׁ֣ר בְּחֶבְר֑וֹן וַיִּֽבֶן־שָׁ֥ם מִזְבֵּ֖חַ לַֽיהוָֽה׃ (פ)

i18n.en: Abram moved his tent, and came and dwelt by the oaks of Mamre, which are in Hebron, and built there an altar to YHWH.

paragraphs.commentary: **The chapter closes by naming a sacred-tree site that will become a recurring locus across the Abraham cycle.** *Elonei Mamre* — 'the oaks of Mamre' (plural construct, אֵלֹנֵי מַמְרֵא) — is morphologically and topographically distinct from the *elon Moreh* (singular construct) of Gen 12:6. The Moreh site is at Shechem in the central hill country and names a tree-by-its-oracle-function (*moreh* = teacher / oracle-giver); the Mamre site is near Hebron in the southern hill country and names a tree-grove by its *human* owner — Mamre the Amorite, named explicitly at Gen 14:13 and 14:24 as one of Abram's three Amorite allies in the war of the four kings. // **The two sacred-tree sites are parallels but not the same entry.** Both fit the patriarchal sacred-tree pattern that also runs through Gen 35:4 (Shechem oak), Gen 35:8 (Allon Bakhut at Bethel), Josh 24:26 (Shechem sanctuary oak), Judg 6:11 (Ophrah oak), and Judg 9:6, 37 (Shechem diviners' oak); both are theophany-and-altar locations. But the proper names track different historical persons / places, and the *elon-moreh* glossary entry from 12:6 does not extend to here. // **The Mamre site is forward-loaded in the narrative.** Abram will dwell there during the war of the four kings (Gen 14:13); the three-visitors theophany of Gen 18:1 (*va-yera elav YHWH b-elonei Mamre*) happens here; the cave of Machpelah purchased by Abraham as the patriarchal-matriarchal burial site (Gen 23:17, 19) is in the field of Ephron near Mamre; the burial-narratives of Sarah (23:19), Abraham (25:9), Isaac and Rebekah (49:31), and Jacob (50:13) all return to Mamre. The chapter's closing notice quietly seeds the geographical anchor of the rest of the cycle. // **On the botanical question** (oak vs. terebinth): BDB, HALOT, and the Hebrew lexica do not securely distinguish *elon* (אֵלוֹן) and *elah* (אֵלָה); LXX renders δρῦς (oak); ASV and NRSV translate 'oaks', NJPS 'terebinths'. The WoH translation follows ASV with 'oaks of Mamre', consistent with the 12:6 'oak of Moreh' rendering. The species precision is not load-bearing.
